skills.hypothesis: A testable, directional hypothesis: if [change], then [variable] will increase or decrease, because ...
skills.variables: The independent and dependent variable the scenario actually measures
skills.control: A control group and what it is for, and a variable held constant
skills.chain: A complete cause-and-effect chain, every link named
skills.trend: A data trend described with numbers and explained
skills.solution: A solution fitted to the scenario: its scale, its constraints, and how it works
skills.policy: A policy (a law or rule) when a policy is asked, not a technology
skills.tradeoff: An advantage and a disadvantage, each with its reason

prompts.title: Explaining a seasonal carbon dioxide cycle
prompts.context: Carbon dioxide in the air at a station in the Northern Hemisphere (invented values for practice, similar in size to real records): May 424 ppm, September 418 ppm, the next May 426 ppm.
prompts.prompt: Describe the pattern in the data and explain what causes the fall from May to September.
checklist: Describes the pattern with numbers: a fall of 6 ppm from May to September, then a rise to 426 ppm the next May
Explains the fall: Northern Hemisphere plants photosynthesize in summer and take carbon dioxide out of the air
Explains the rise: in winter photosynthesis slows while respiration and decomposition keep releasing carbon dioxide

earns.answer: Carbon dioxide fell from 424 ppm in May to 418 ppm in September, a drop of 6 ppm, then rose to 426 ppm the next May. The summer fall happens because Northern Hemisphere plants photosynthesize most in summer and take in more carbon dioxide than respiration releases. In winter, photosynthesis slows while respiration and decomposition continue, so carbon dioxide builds up again.
earns.why: It gives the numbers, names the cause of each part of the cycle and the process behind it.

misses.answer: Carbon dioxide goes down and then up again because of the seasons.
misses.why: No numbers, and "the seasons" is not a mechanism; it never names photosynthesis or respiration.

prompts.title: The control in a nitrogen-fixing experiment
prompts.context: A class grows bean plants in sterile soil. Half the pots get soil bacteria that fix nitrogen in the bean roots; half get none. All pots get the same water, light and soil, and no fertilizer. After six weeks the class weighs the plants (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the control group and describe its purpose. Then identify one variable held constant.
checklist: Names the control: the pots of beans with no nitrogen-fixing bacteria added
Says what the control is for: a baseline to compare the plants with bacteria against
Names a constant: water, light, soil type or the amount of fertilizer (none)

earns.answer: The control group is the pots that get no nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Its purpose is to give a baseline: comparing their mass with the plants that got bacteria shows how much growth the bacteria cause. The amount of water each pot gets is held constant.
earns.why: It names the control, says what it is for (a baseline that isolates the effect of the bacteria) and names a constant.

misses.answer: The control is the beans without bacteria, and the water is the same.
misses.why: It names the control but never says what it is for, and an exam reader gives a point only when the purpose is stated.

control.label: Control group
options: the pots with no nitrogen-fixing bacteria
the plants that grow the most

why.1: Those pots get the treatment; the control is left without it.
why.2: The control is set before the results, not chosen from them.

purpose.label: Its purpose
options: a baseline to compare against, so any extra growth can be traced to the bacteria
to make the plants grow faster
to give the bacteria more food

why.1: The control is not meant to grow faster; it shows growth without the treatment.
why.2: The control pots have no bacteria to feed.

constant.label: A constant
options: the amount of water each pot gets

why.1: That is what the class changes, the independent variable.
why.2: That is what the class measures, the dependent variable.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about light and pond algae
prompts.context: A student fills six clear bottles with pond water and algae. Two sit in full sun, two under one layer of shade cloth, and two under three layers. After 24 hours she measures the oxygen each bottle produced, to compare the algae's productivity (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this experiment.
checklist: Names the change the student makes: the amount of light the bottles get
Names what is measured: the oxygen the algae produce (their productivity)
Gives a direction: oxygen production will increase or decrease, not just change
Gives a reason that names photosynthesis or how light drives it

earns.answer: If the bottles receive more light, then the algae will produce more oxygen, because light is the energy source for photosynthesis, which makes oxygen.
earns.why: It names the change (more light), the measured variable (oxygen produced), a direction (more) and the reason (light drives photosynthesis).

misses.answer: Light will affect how much oxygen the algae make in the bottles.
misses.why: "Affect" gives no direction, so no result could prove it wrong, and there is no reason.

change.label: If ...
options: the bottles hold more pond water
the bottles are left out longer

why.1: The water volume is the same in every bottle; the student changes the light.
why.2: Every bottle runs for the same 24 hours; time is held constant.

why.1: Color is not measured; the student records oxygen produced.
why.2: Room temperature is not what the student measures.

why.1: More light gives more energy for photosynthesis, so oxygen should rise, not fall.
why.2: "Change" gives no direction; a hypothesis says which way.

because.label: because ...
options: light is the energy source for photosynthesis, which makes oxygen
shade cloth adds oxygen to the water

why.1: A preference is not a mechanism; name the process light powers.
why.2: Shade cloth adds nothing to the water; it only blocks light.

prompts.title: The variables in a grassland watering study
prompts.context: Ecologists water 12 grassland plots with 0, 10, 20 or 30 mm of extra water a week. At the end of summer they clip, dry and weigh the plants in each plot, in grams per square meter (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this study.
checklist: Independent variable: the amount of extra water added each week (0 to 30 mm)
Dependent variable: the dry mass of plants per square meter, a measure of productivity
Uses the variable the study actually measures, not a related one such as rainfall or plant height

earns.answer: The independent variable is the amount of extra water each plot gets per week, from 0 to 30 mm. The dependent variable is the dry plant mass in grams per square meter at the end of summer, which measures the plots' productivity.
earns.why: Both variables are named exactly as the study sets and measures them, with their units.

misses.answer: The independent variable is rain and the dependent variable is how tall the grass grows.
misses.why: The ecologists add water; they do not change rainfall. And they weigh dry plants, they do not measure height.

iv.label: Independent variable
options: the amount of extra water added each week
the dry plant mass per square meter

why.1: That is what is measured at the end, the dependent variable.
why.2: The plot count is part of the design, not the variable that is changed.

dv.label: Dependent variable
options: the dry plant mass per square meter
the amount of rain that fell

why.1: Height is not measured; the plants are clipped, dried and weighed.
why.2: Rainfall is not measured or controlled; extra water is added.

prompts.title: Why there are so few top predators
prompts.prompt: Explain why a grassland supports thousands of grazing animals but only a few wolves.
checklist: Producers capture energy from sunlight, and only part of it passes to grazers
At each step most energy is used in respiration and lost as heat; only about 10% is passed on
So little energy is left at the top level, which can support only a few predators

earns.answer: Grasses capture energy from sunlight. When grazers eat them, only about 10% of the grasses' energy becomes grazer tissue, because most is used in respiration and lost as heat. The same loss happens again when wolves eat the grazers, so the wolves' level gets only about 1% of the grasses' energy, which can support only a few wolves.
earns.why: Every link is there: the source, the 10% passed on, why the rest is lost (respiration and heat) and what that means for the top level.

misses.answer: There are fewer wolves because wolves are at the top of the food chain and need to eat a lot.
misses.why: It restates the question. It never says that energy is lost as heat at each level, which is the reason.

prompts.title: Draining a wetland for farmland
prompts.prompt: Describe one economic advantage and one environmental disadvantage of draining a wetland to grow crops, each with its reason.
checklist: Gives an advantage with its reason: new cropland earns income from food sold
Gives a disadvantage that is a lost ecosystem service, with how the wetland provided it
Each point says why, not just names a word

earns.answer: Advantage: the drained land can grow crops, so the farmer earns income from food that land produced nothing to sell before. Disadvantage: the town loses flood control, because the wetland held storm water like a sponge and released it slowly; once it is drained, rain runs off quickly and floods land downstream.
earns.why: Each side has its reason, and the disadvantage names the ecosystem service and how it worked.

misses.answer: It makes money but it is bad for the environment and the animals.
misses.why: "Bad for the environment" names no service and no mechanism, and the advantage has no reason.

prompts.title: Island size and species
prompts.context: Bird species counted on four islands the same distance from the mainland (invented data for practice): 2 km², 9 species; 20 km², 18 species; 200 km², 35 species; 2,000 km², 70 species.
prompts.prompt: Describe the relationship in the data and explain it.
checklist: Describes the trend with numbers: species rise from 9 to 70 as area rises from 2 to 2,000 km²
Notes the pattern: each tenfold rise in area roughly doubles the number of species
Explains it: larger islands have more habitats and larger populations, so fewer species go extinct

earns.answer: Larger islands have more bird species: 9 species on 2 km² but 70 on 2,000 km². Each tenfold increase in area about doubles the species count (9, 18, 35, 70). Larger islands hold more kinds of habitat and larger populations, so their extinction rates are lower and more species persist.
earns.why: It describes the trend with the data, adds the doubling pattern and gives the mechanism (habitat and extinction).

misses.answer: Bigger islands have more birds on them because there is more room.
misses.why: It confuses birds with bird species, gives no numbers, and "more room" skips habitats and extinction rates.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about trout and warm water
prompts.context: A biologist keeps young brook trout in tanks at 12, 16, 20 and 24 °C for 30 days and counts how many survive in each tank (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this study.
checklist: Names the change: water temperature
Names what is measured: the number of trout that survive
Gives a direction for the result
Gives a reason based on the trout's range of tolerance

earns.answer: If the water temperature is raised above the trout's optimal range, then fewer trout will survive, because warm water is outside their range of tolerance and puts them under physiological stress.
earns.why: A statement with the change, the measured variable, a direction and a reason tied to the range of tolerance.

misses.answer: How does water temperature impact the number of trout that survive?
misses.why: It is a question, and "impact" gives no direction to test.

change.label: If ...
options: more trout are added to each tank

why.1: Tank size is the same throughout; temperature is what changes.
why.2: Each tank starts with the same number of trout.

measure.label: then ...
options: the trout will affect the water

why.1: Color is not measured; survival is.
why.2: This gives neither the measured variable nor a direction.

because.label: because ...
options: warm water is outside the trout's range of tolerance
warm water has more food in it

why.1: Liking is not a reason a reader accepts; name the tolerance range or the stress.
why.2: Food is not part of the study, and it would not explain fewer survivors.

prompts.title: Protecting a beach town from storm flooding
prompts.context: A beach town loses houses when storm waves flood the shore. The town cannot afford a concrete seawall and wants a solution other than moving the houses.
prompts.prompt: Propose a solution that fits these constraints and explain how it works.
checklist: Proposes a low-cost option other than a seawall or moving houses (for example, rebuilding and planting dunes, or restoring a salt marsh)
Explains how it works: how it reduces the force or reach of the storm waves
Fits the town's scale and stated constraints

earns.answer: Rebuild the sand dunes in front of the houses and plant them with dune grass. The grass roots hold the sand in place, and the dunes act as a barrier that absorbs wave energy and blocks the flooding waves before they reach the houses, at much lower cost than a seawall.
earns.why: It respects both constraints and explains the mechanism (roots hold sand, dunes absorb wave energy).

misses.answer: Build a seawall to stop the waves from hitting the houses.
misses.why: The question rules out a seawall, and the reader gives no point for a solution the stem excludes.

solution.label: Solution
options: rebuild the dunes and plant them with dune grass

why.1: The town cannot afford a seawall.
why.2: The question asks for something other than moving the houses.

how.label: How it works
options: roots hold the sand, and the dunes absorb wave energy before it reaches the houses
it makes the beach look nicer for tourists

why.1: Looks are not a way of stopping a surge.
why.2: No local project stops storms forming; it can only reduce their damage.

prompts.title: From burned forest back to forest
prompts.context: A fire burns a forest but leaves its soil in place.
prompts.prompt: Explain how the area returns to forest, naming each stage.
checklist: Names it secondary succession, since the soil remained
Pioneer plants (grasses, weeds) grow first from seeds and roots in the soil
Shrubs and fast-growing trees shade out the pioneers; later, shade-tolerant trees replace them as the soil deepens
Ends with a mature forest community

earns.answer: This is secondary succession, because the soil was not destroyed. Grasses and weeds sprout first from seeds and roots left in the soil. They add organic matter, and shrubs and fast-growing, sun-loving trees move in and shade them out. Over decades, shade-tolerant trees grow up under those trees and replace them, until a mature forest returns.
earns.why: It names the kind of succession with its reason and every stage in order, each with why it gives way to the next.

misses.answer: The forest grows back over time through primary succession.
misses.why: Soil remained, so it is secondary succession, and no stages are named.

prompts.title: A deer population that crashed
prompts.context: Deer on an island (invented data for practice): 1990, 200; 2000, 1,400; 2005, 2,000; 2008, 500.
prompts.prompt: Describe the trend with numbers and explain what happened.
checklist: Describes the growth: from 200 to 2,000 deer by 2005, a tenfold rise
Describes the crash: down to 500 by 2008, a 75% drop
Explains it: the herd overshot the island's carrying capacity, overused its food, and died back

earns.answer: The herd grew from 200 deer in 1990 to 2,000 in 2005, ten times as many, then fell to 500 in 2008, a drop of 75%. The herd overshot the island's carrying capacity: with more deer than the plants could support, the deer ate their food faster than it regrew, and many starved, so the population died back.
earns.why: It gives both parts of the trend with numbers (including the percent drop) and explains overshoot and dieback.

misses.answer: The deer went up and then down because there were too many deer.
misses.why: No numbers, and "too many deer" never names carrying capacity or the loss of food that caused the crash.

prompts.title: The variables in a duckweed study
prompts.context: Students grow duckweed in 12 cups of pond water, adding 0, 1, 2 or 4 drops of plant fertilizer to each. Every three days for three weeks they count the duckweed fronds in each cup (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable, and describe what the results test.
checklist: Independent variable: drops of fertilizer added (the nutrients available)
Dependent variable: the number of duckweed fronds counted
Says the study tests whether more nutrients let the population grow faster or reach a higher carrying capacity

earns.answer: The independent variable is the number of drops of fertilizer added to each cup, which sets the nutrients available. The dependent variable is the number of duckweed fronds counted every three days. The study tests whether more nutrients make the population grow faster and level off at a higher carrying capacity.
earns.why: It names both variables as the study sets and counts them, and says what the results can show.

misses.answer: The independent variable is time and the dependent variable is the duckweed.
misses.why: Time is when the counts are taken, not what the students change, and "the duckweed" is not a measurement.

why.1: Time is when counts are taken; the students change the fertilizer.
why.2: The number of fronds is what is measured.

dv.label: Dependent variable
options: the number of duckweed fronds counted

why.1: Fertilizer is what is changed.
why.2: Every cup is the same size; that is a constant.

prompts.title: A policy to lower a high fertility rate
prompts.context: A country with a total fertility rate of 5.8 wants to slow its population growth without limiting the number of children a family may have.
prompts.prompt: Propose a policy that fits this constraint and explain how it would lower the fertility rate.
checklist: Proposes a policy (a law, program or rule), not a technology or a personal choice
Respects the constraint: no limit on family size
Explains how it lowers fertility (for example, more years in school delay marriage and first births)

earns.answer: Pass a law that makes secondary school free and required for girls. Girls who stay in school marry and have their first child later, and educated women have more job opportunities and better access to family planning, so they tend to choose smaller families, which lowers the total fertility rate.
earns.why: It is a policy, it respects the constraint, and it explains the mechanism step by step.

misses.answer: Give out more birth control so people have fewer babies.
misses.why: That names a technology, not a policy, and does not say how the country would carry it out.

type.label: A policy is
options: a law that makes secondary school free and required for girls
a one-child limit for every family

why.1: That is a technology; the question asks for a policy.
why.2: The question rules out limiting family size.

how.label: It works because
options: girls who stay in school marry later and choose smaller families
it makes children cost less to raise

why.1: Land use has nothing to do with fertility.
why.2: Cheaper children would tend to raise fertility, not lower it.

prompts.title: When a city will double
prompts.context: A city of 2 million people grows at 1.75% per year (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Calculate the year, starting in 2025, when the city will reach 4 million if the rate stays the same, then explain one reason the real year may differ.
checklist: Uses the rule of 70: 70 / 1.75 = 40 years
Adds the doubling time to the start year: 2025 + 40 = 2065, and says 4 million is double 2 million
Gives a reason the rate may change (falling fertility, migration, a disaster), with its effect on the year

earns.answer: Doubling time = 70 / 1.75 = 40 years. Since 4 million is double 2 million, the city reaches it in 2025 + 40 = 2065. The real year may be later: if the city's fertility rate keeps falling, its growth rate will drop below 1.75% and doubling will take longer.
earns.why: It shows the rule of 70 with its numbers, adds the doubling time to the start year, and explains a reason the rate could change.

misses.answer: 70 / 1.75 = 40, so it takes 40 years for the city to double.
misses.why: It stops at the doubling time; the question asks for the year, so 40 must be added to 2025, and the reason is missing.

prompts.title: Why death rates fall before birth rates
prompts.prompt: Explain why, in stage 2 of the demographic transition, the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high, and what this does to the population.
checklist: Death rate falls first: better food supply, clean water, sanitation and medicine reduce deaths, especially of children
Birth rate stays high: families still expect children to work and support parents, and customs change slowly
Result: births far exceed deaths, so the population grows quickly

earns.answer: In stage 2, food supply, clean water, sanitation and medicine improve, so fewer people die, especially children, and the death rate falls. The birth rate stays high because families still rely on children for farm work and support in old age, and customs about family size change slowly. With births far above deaths, the rate of natural increase is high and the population grows rapidly.
earns.why: Each part has its cause, and it ends with the effect on population growth.

misses.answer: The death rate falls because of better health care, and then the population grows.
misses.why: It never explains why the birth rate stays high, which is the link that makes the population grow.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about plant cover and soil loss
prompts.context: A class builds four trays of the same soil on the same slope. One tray is bare; the others have 25%, 50% or 100% grass cover. The class pours the same amount of water over each tray and weighs the soil that washes off (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this experiment.
checklist: Names the change: the percent of grass cover
Names what is measured: the mass of soil washed off
Gives a direction for the result: an increase or a decrease
Gives a reason: roots hold soil and plants slow the water

earns.answer: If the grass cover on the soil is increased, then less soil will wash off the tray, because grass roots hold the soil together and the leaves slow the water running over it.
earns.why: Statement, change, measured variable, direction and mechanism are all there.

misses.answer: Grass cover will change the amount of soil that washes off.
misses.why: "Change" gives no direction and there is no reason.

why.1: Every tray sits on the same slope.
why.2: The same amount of water goes on each tray.

why.1: Plant cover protects soil; more cover should mean less loss.
why.2: A hypothesis states a direction, not just a change.

because.label: because ...
options: roots hold the soil and plants slow the running water

why.1: Weight is not why vegetation protects soil.
why.2: Plants do not absorb all the water; they slow it and anchor the soil.

prompts.title: Saving soil on a sloping farm
prompts.context: A farmer grows corn on a hillside and loses soil in every heavy rain. The farmer wants to keep growing corn on the same field.
prompts.prompt: Propose a practice that fits this constraint and explain how it reduces erosion.
checklist: Proposes a practice that keeps corn on the field (for example, planting rows across the slope, or leaving crop stalks on the ground between seasons)
Explains how it works: slows runoff or holds soil
Fits the stated constraint

earns.answer: Plant the corn rows across the slope, following its level lines, instead of up and down the hill. Each row then forms a small ridge across the slope that slows running water and traps soil, so less soil washes downhill while the farmer keeps growing corn.
earns.why: It keeps the crop, and it explains how the ridges slow water and trap soil.

misses.answer: The farmer should plant trees on the hillside instead of corn.
misses.why: The farmer wants to keep growing corn, so a solution that replaces it ignores the constraint.

prompts.title: A fair test of how fast water soaks in
prompts.context: A student pours 500 mL of water into a tube pushed into three soils (sandy, loam and clay) and times how long it takes to soak in (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify two variables the student must hold constant and explain why each matters.
checklist: Names a constant: the volume of water poured (500 mL)
Names a second constant: the tube size, the depth it is pushed in, or how dry the soil is at the start
Explains that keeping them the same means differences in time come from the soil type alone

earns.answer: The student must use the same volume of water, 500 mL, each time, and push the tube to the same depth in each soil. If either changed, the soak-in time would change for reasons other than the soil, so keeping them constant means any difference in time comes from the soil's texture.
earns.why: Two constants, each with its reason (isolating the soil type as the cause).

misses.answer: Keep everything the same in each test so the experiment is fair.
misses.why: It names no variable, and the point goes only to a named constant with its reason.

prompts.title: How a rain shadow forms
prompts.prompt: Explain why the windward side of a coastal mountain range is wet and the leeward side is dry.
checklist: Moist air from the ocean is pushed up the windward slope
Rising air cools, water vapor condenses, and rain or snow falls on the windward side
The air that crosses the peaks has lost its moisture; it sinks and warms on the leeward side, so little rain falls there

earns.answer: Wind pushes moist ocean air up the windward slope. As the air rises it cools, its water vapor condenses into clouds, and rain or snow falls on that side. The air that crosses the peaks has lost most of its moisture, and as it sinks down the leeward side it warms, which keeps water from condensing, so the leeward side is dry.
earns.why: Every link: rising, cooling, condensing, losing moisture, sinking and warming.

misses.answer: The mountains block the rain, so one side is wet and one is dry.
misses.why: "Block the rain" skips the mechanism: rising air cools and drops its moisture.

prompts.title: Water temperature and the anchovy catch
prompts.context: Off the coast of Peru (invented data for practice): in a normal year, surface water 19 °C and anchovy catch 8 million metric tons; in an El Niño year, 24 °C and 2 million metric tons.
prompts.prompt: Describe the relationship in the data and explain it.
checklist: Describes it with numbers: water 5 °C warmer in the El Niño year, catch down by 6 million metric tons (75% lower)
Explains: weaker trade winds slow the upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water
Links fewer nutrients to less plankton and fewer anchovies

earns.answer: In the El Niño year the water was 5 °C warmer (24 °C versus 19 °C) and the catch fell from 8 to 2 million metric tons, 75% lower. During El Niño the trade winds weaken, so less cold, nutrient-rich water wells up along the coast. With fewer nutrients, less plankton grows, and the anchovies that feed on it decline.
earns.why: The trend with numbers, then each link from wind to fish.

misses.answer: When it is El Niño the water is warmer so the fish don't like it and leave.
misses.why: No numbers, and "don't like it" skips the real link: less upwelling, fewer nutrients, less plankton.

prompts.title: From clearcutting to a muddy stream
prompts.prompt: Explain how clearcutting a steep forested slope can harm fish in the stream below.
checklist: Removing the trees removes the roots that held the soil
Rain erodes the bare soil and carries sediment into the stream
Sediment makes the water cloudy and buries gravel beds, and loss of shade warms the water
Fish lose spawning sites or are stressed, so their numbers fall

earns.answer: Clearcutting removes the trees and, as the roots die, nothing holds the soil. Rain washes the bare soil downhill, and sediment flows into the stream. The sediment clouds the water and fills the gravel beds where fish lay eggs, and without the trees' shade the water warms. Fish lose places to spawn, so fewer young survive.
earns.why: Each link is named, from roots to soil to sediment to the fish.

misses.answer: Clearcutting causes erosion, which is bad for fish.
misses.why: It skips the links: how erosion gets to the stream and what sediment does to the fish.

prompts.title: Saving water on a dry farm
prompts.context: A farmer in a dry region irrigates vegetables by flooding the furrows. Groundwater is falling. The farmer will keep the same crops and wants to use less water.
prompts.prompt: Propose an irrigation method that fits these constraints and explain how it saves water.
checklist: Proposes drip irrigation (or another targeted method) and keeps the same crops
Explains how it saves water: delivers water to the roots, so less evaporates or runs off
Connects the saving to the falling groundwater

earns.answer: Switch from furrow irrigation to drip irrigation. Drip tubes deliver water slowly right at each plant's roots, so far less evaporates from the soil surface or runs off the field. The farmer grows the same vegetables with less water and pumps less groundwater, which slows the drop in the water table.
earns.why: It fits both constraints and explains how the water is saved.

misses.answer: Use less water by growing crops that need less water, like cactus.
misses.why: The farmer will keep the same crops, so changing crops ignores the constraint, and it names no method.

method.label: Method
options: switching to a crop that needs less water

why.1: Flooding is what the farmer already does; it wastes water.
why.2: The farmer will keep the same crops.

how.label: How it saves water
options: water goes straight to the roots, so less evaporates or runs off
it adds nutrients to the soil

why.1: Drip irrigation saves water, not by cleaning it.
why.2: Nutrients are not how drip irrigation saves water.

prompts.title: A policy against overfishing
prompts.context: Cod in a fishing ground have fallen to a tenth of their numbers 30 years ago.
prompts.prompt: Propose a policy to help the cod recover and explain how it works.
checklist: Proposes a policy (a law, quota or rule), not a technology
Explains how it lets the population recover
Is specific to the cod fishery

earns.answer: Set a law that limits each year's cod catch to a quota scientists set below the population's growth, and close spawning grounds in the spawning season. Fewer adult cod are taken and more spawn, so births exceed deaths and the population can grow back.
earns.why: It is a rule, it is specific, and it explains how fewer fish caught means more spawning and recovery.

misses.answer: Use nets with bigger holes so small fish can escape.
misses.why: Bigger mesh is a technology. A policy would be a law requiring larger mesh, and it needs the how.

type.label: A policy is
options: a law setting a yearly catch quota

why.1: That is gear, a technology. A law requiring it would be a policy.
why.2: That is a technology, and it would raise the catch.

how.label: It works because
options: fewer adults are caught, so more spawn and the population grows
it moves the cod to a new ocean

why.1: Taste has nothing to do with recovery.
why.2: A quota does not move fish.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about permeable pavement
prompts.context: A city covers half of a parking lot with permeable pavement and leaves half as ordinary asphalt. Gauges measure how much water runs off each half after storms (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this study.
checklist: Names the change: permeable pavement instead of asphalt
Names the measure: the volume of runoff
Gives a direction for the result: an increase or a decrease
Gives a reason: water soaks through permeable pavement into the ground

earns.answer: If a parking area is covered with permeable pavement instead of asphalt, then less water will run off it after a storm, because rain soaks through the pavement into the ground instead of flowing over it.
earns.why: Statement, change, measure, direction and mechanism.

misses.answer: Does permeable pavement make a difference to how much water runs off?
misses.why: It is a question, not a statement, and it gives no direction to test.

change.label: If ...
options: the parking area has permeable pavement instead of asphalt
the parking lot is made larger
more cars park on the lot

why.1: Lot size is fixed; the surface is what changes.
why.2: Cars are not part of the study.

why.1: Permeable pavement lets water soak in, so runoff should fall.
why.2: A hypothesis says which way.

because.label: because ...
options: rain soaks through the pavement into the ground

why.1: Age of the pavement is not the mechanism.
why.2: Pavement does not evaporate water; the water soaks through.

prompts.title: Integrated pest management on an orchard
prompts.prompt: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of an apple orchard switching from regular spraying to integrated pest management (IPM).
checklist: Advantage with reason: fewer pesticide applications, so less harm to pollinators, less runoff and less pesticide resistance
Disadvantage with reason: IPM takes more time, monitoring and training, or can cost more at first
Each side explains its reason

earns.answer: Advantage: the grower sprays only when monitoring shows pests above a threshold, so less pesticide reaches bees and nearby streams, and pests are slower to evolve resistance. Disadvantage: IPM takes more labor and knowledge, because someone must check traps and leaves every week and choose among biological, cultural and chemical controls, which raises costs at first.
earns.why: Both sides are named with the reason each happens.

misses.answer: IPM is better for the environment but it is harder.
misses.why: "Better" and "harder" name no specific benefit or cost, and give no reasons.

prompts.title: A country's energy use
prompts.context: Energy use in a developing country (invented data for practice): 2000, 4 exajoules; 2010, 6 exajoules; 2020, 10 exajoules.
prompts.prompt: Describe the trend with a calculation and explain one likely cause.
checklist: Calculates the percent change: (10 - 4) / 4 × 100 = 150% from 2000 to 2020
Describes the speed-up: a rise of 2 exajoules in the first decade and 4 in the second
Gives a cause linked to development (industry, cars, electricity reaching more homes, a growing population)

earns.answer: Energy use rose by (10 - 4) / 4 × 100 = 150% from 2000 to 2020, and the rise sped up: 2 exajoules in the first decade and 4 in the second. As the country develops, more homes get electricity, factories grow and more people own cars, so energy use per person rises along with the population.
earns.why: The trend with a correct percent change and the speed-up, then a cause tied to development.

misses.answer: Energy use went up by 6, from 4 exajoules to 10 exajoules.
misses.why: 6 exajoules is the change, not a percent change, and there is no cause.

prompts.title: Switching a power plant from coal to natural gas
prompts.prompt: Describe one environmental advantage and one environmental disadvantage of converting a coal power plant to natural gas.
checklist: Advantage with reason: natural gas releases about half the carbon dioxide per kWh, and less soot and sulfur
Disadvantage with reason: methane leaks from wells and pipelines, or hydraulic fracturing can contaminate groundwater
Does not call natural gas zero emissions

earns.answer: Advantage: burning natural gas releases about half the carbon dioxide of coal per kWh, and far less of the soot and sulfur that coal smoke carries. Disadvantage: methane leaks from wells and pipelines, and methane is a powerful heat-trapping gas, so leaks cancel part of the benefit.
earns.why: Each side is specific and has its reason, and it never calls gas clean or zero emissions.

misses.answer: Natural gas is clean so it has no emissions, but it is still a fossil fuel.
misses.why: Natural gas does release carbon dioxide, so "no emissions" is wrong, and the disadvantage has no reason.

prompts.title: The variables in a solar panel test
prompts.context: A student tilts a small solar panel at 0°, 15°, 30°, 45° and 60° toward the south at noon and records the electricity it produces in watts (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables and one variable to hold constant.
checklist: Independent variable: the tilt angle of the panel
Dependent variable: the electrical power produced, in watts
Constant: same panel, same time of day, same day or sky conditions

earns.answer: The independent variable is the panel's tilt angle, from 0° to 60°. The dependent variable is the electrical power it produces, in watts. The time of day must stay the same (noon) for every reading, so the sun's position does not change.
earns.why: Both variables with units, and a constant with its reason.

misses.answer: The independent variable is the sun and the dependent variable is the solar panel.
misses.why: The student changes the angle, not the sun, and the panel is equipment, not a measurement.

iv.label: Independent variable
options: the tilt angle of the panel

why.1: That is the measured result.
why.2: Time is held constant at noon.

dv.label: Dependent variable
options: the power the panel produces, in watts

why.1: The angle is what is changed.
why.2: The same panel is used throughout.

why.1: That is the independent variable.
why.2: That is the dependent variable.

prompts.title: How a dam affects salmon
prompts.prompt: Explain how building a hydroelectric dam on a river can reduce its salmon population.
checklist: The dam blocks adults swimming upstream to spawn
The reservoir slows and warms the water, and young salmon swimming downstream are hurt by turbines or delayed
Fewer salmon reach spawning grounds or survive to the sea, so the population falls

earns.answer: The dam is a wall across the river, so adult salmon swimming upstream to spawn cannot reach the gravel beds above it. Above the dam the reservoir is slow and warm, and young salmon heading to the sea are delayed or killed in the turbines. With fewer adults spawning and fewer young surviving, the population declines.
earns.why: Each link from the dam to the population is named, for both adults and young.

misses.answer: Dams are bad for fish because they change the river.
misses.why: "Change the river" names no mechanism and no link to spawning or survival.

prompts.title: A policy to cut home energy use
prompts.context: A state wants to reduce the energy its homes use for heating and cooling.
prompts.prompt: Propose a policy and explain how it reduces energy use.
checklist: Proposes a policy (law, rule, tax credit), not just a technology
Explains how it reduces energy use
Is specific to heating and cooling homes

earns.answer: Pass a building code requiring new homes to have insulated walls and attics and double-pane windows, and give tax credits for adding insulation to older homes. Insulation slows heat flowing through walls and roofs, so furnaces and air conditioners run less to keep the same temperature.
earns.why: A law and a tax credit, specific to heating and cooling, with how insulation saves energy.

misses.answer: People should use LED light bulbs and turn off the lights.
misses.why: LEDs are a technology and lighting is not heating or cooling; the question asks for a policy.

type.label: A policy is
options: a building code requiring insulation in new homes

why.1: That is a technology; a law requiring it would be the policy.
why.2: That is a personal choice, not a law or rule.

how.label: It works because
options: insulation slows heat flow, so heating and cooling run less

why.1: Appearance does not save energy.
why.2: The code does not change the price of electricity.

prompts.title: How a sunny day makes ozone
prompts.prompt: Explain how morning traffic in a sunny city leads to high ground-level ozone in the afternoon.
checklist: Cars emit nitrogen oxides (NO) and volatile organic compounds during the morning rush
NO is oxidized to nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and sunlight splits NO2, freeing oxygen atoms
The oxygen atoms join oxygen molecules to form ozone, and VOCs keep NO from destroying it, so ozone builds to a peak in the afternoon

earns.answer: In the morning rush hour, cars emit nitrogen oxide and VOCs. The nitrogen oxide turns into nitrogen dioxide, and as the sun climbs, sunlight splits nitrogen dioxide into nitrogen oxide and a free oxygen atom, which joins an oxygen molecule to form ozone. Radicals from VOCs turn nitrogen oxide back into nitrogen dioxide without using up ozone, so ozone builds through the day and peaks in the afternoon.
earns.why: Every link: the emissions, sunlight splitting NO2, ozone forming, and why it accumulates.

misses.answer: Cars give off ozone, which builds up during the day.
misses.why: Cars do not emit ozone; it is a secondary pollutant made by sunlight acting on their emissions.

prompts.title: Radon in a basement
prompts.context: A family finds high radon levels in their basement bedroom. They cannot move.
prompts.prompt: Propose a solution that fits their situation and explain how it lowers the radon.
checklist: Proposes a fix that keeps the family in the house (seal cracks, install a vent pipe and fan under the floor)
Explains how it works: blocks radon entering from the rock and soil, or removes it before it gets in
Fits the stated constraint

earns.answer: Seal the cracks in the basement floor and walls and install a vent pipe with a fan that draws air from under the floor and blows it outside above the roof. Radon gas from the rock below is pulled away before it can seep into the house, so it reduces indoor radon levels.
earns.why: It fits the constraint and explains how radon is kept out.

misses.answer: Open the windows sometimes to let fresh air in.
misses.why: Vague (how often, which windows?), and it never says how the radon, which seeps up from the ground, is stopped.

solution.label: Solution
options: seal floor cracks and add a vent fan that draws air from under the floor
buy an air purifier with a carbon filter

why.1: The family cannot move.
why.2: Ordinary room purifiers do little against radon gas; the fix is to keep it out.

how.label: How it works
options: it pulls radon from the soil outside before it enters the house
it makes the radon less radioactive
it adds more oxygen to the room

why.1: Nothing in a home changes how radioactive radon is.
why.2: Oxygen does not cancel radon.

prompts.title: Cutting sulfur dioxide from power plants
prompts.prompt: Propose a policy to reduce sulfur dioxide from coal power plants and explain how it works.
checklist: Proposes a policy, a law or rule (an emissions cap, a cap-and-trade program, a law requiring scrubbers), not just a device
Explains how it cuts emissions
Names sulfur dioxide and the plants it targets

earns.answer: Pass a law that caps total sulfur dioxide from power plants and lets plants trade permits. Each plant must cut its emissions (for example by installing scrubbers or burning low-sulfur coal) or buy permits from plants that cut more, so total sulfur dioxide falls to the cap at the lowest cost.
earns.why: A policy, with how the cap forces emissions down.

misses.answer: Power plants should use scrubbers in their smokestacks.
misses.why: Scrubbers are a technology. The policy would be a law requiring them, or a cap that makes plants choose them.

type.label: A policy is
options: a law that caps sulfur dioxide and lets plants trade permits

why.1: That is a device, a technology.
why.2: That is an action a plant takes, not a law or rule.

how.label: It works because
options: plants must cut emissions or buy permits, so the total falls to the cap
it makes the smoke a different color
it moves the plants farther away

why.1: Color is not the point.
why.2: Moving plants does not reduce emissions.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about lakes and acid rain
prompts.context: Researchers measure the pH of 20 lakes that receive the same acid rain. Half sit on limestone bedrock and half on granite (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this study.
checklist: Names the change: limestone versus granite bedrock
Names the measure: lake pH
Gives a direction: higher pH (less acidic) on limestone
Gives a reason: limestone neutralizes (buffers) the acid

earns.answer: If a lake sits on limestone bedrock rather than granite, then its pH will be higher, because limestone neutralizes acid from the rain and granite does not.
earns.why: Statement, change, measured variable, direction and reason.

misses.answer: The kind of rock under each lake affects its pH.
misses.why: "Affects" gives no direction to test, and there is no reason why the rock matters.

change.label: If ...
options: a lake sits on limestone rather than granite

why.1: Lake size is not the variable.
why.2: Fish are not part of the study.

why.1: Limestone neutralizes acid, which raises pH.
why.2: "Change" gives no direction; a hypothesis says which way.

why.1: Hardness does not neutralize acid.
why.2: Bedrock does not change rainfall.

prompts.title: A control in a traffic noise study
prompts.context: A scientist plays recorded highway noise near nests in one forest and records how often birds sing. Birds at nests in a second, similar forest hear no recording (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the control group, describe its purpose, and identify one variable to hold constant.
checklist: Control group: birds at nests in the forest with no recorded noise
Purpose: a baseline to compare with, so any change in singing can be traced to the noise
A constant: species of bird, time of day, season or habitat

earns.answer: The control group is the birds in the second forest that hear no recording. They give a baseline: comparing their singing with the birds hearing highway noise shows whether the noise changes how often birds sing. The time of day of the recordings must be the same in both forests.
earns.why: It names the control, says what it is for (a baseline) and gives a constant.

misses.answer: The control is the quiet forest with no highway noise.
misses.why: It names the control but gives neither its purpose (a baseline) nor a constant.

prompts.title: From fertilizer to a dead zone
prompts.prompt: Explain how fertilizer running off farms can lead to fish dying in a lake.
checklist: Nitrate and phosphate run off fields into the lake
The nutrients cause an algal bloom
The algae die, and decomposers break them down, using up dissolved oxygen
Dissolved oxygen falls too low (hypoxia), so fish die

earns.answer: Rain washes nitrate and phosphate from fertilizer into the lake. These nutrients cause an algal bloom. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up dissolved oxygen in the water. Oxygen falls so low that fish cannot breathe, and they die.
earns.why: Every link is there, in order, with decomposition as the step that uses the oxygen.

misses.answer: Fertilizer gets in the lake and makes algae grow, which kills the fish.
misses.why: It skips the key links: algae die, decomposers use up oxygen, and low oxygen kills the fish.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about warm water and oxygen
prompts.context: A class heats samples of river water to 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C and measures the dissolved oxygen in each (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this experiment.
checklist: Names the change: water temperature
Names the measure: dissolved oxygen
Gives a direction for the result: an increase or a decrease
Gives a reason: warmer water holds less dissolved gas

earns.answer: If the water temperature is increased, then the dissolved oxygen in the water will decrease, because warm water can hold less dissolved gas than cold water.
earns.why: It names the change, the measured variable, a direction and the reason.

misses.answer: If the river water is warmer, the oxygen in it will be different.
misses.why: "Different" gives no direction, and there is no reason.

why.1: Volume is not the variable.
why.2: Stirring is not what changes between samples.

why.1: Warm water holds less dissolved gas, so oxygen should fall.
why.2: "Change" gives no direction; a hypothesis says which way.

because.label: because ...
options: warm water holds less dissolved gas
heat adds chemicals to the water

why.1: Thermal pollution is heat, not chemicals.
why.2: No fish are in the samples.

prompts.title: Mercury up a food chain
prompts.context: Mercury in a lake food chain (invented data for practice): water 0.00002 ppm; plankton 0.002 ppm; small fish 0.02 ppm; pike 0.2 ppm.
prompts.prompt: Describe the pattern and explain it.
checklist: Describes the pattern: the concentration rises 10 times at each level from plankton to pike
Calculates the overall rise: pike carry 100 times the plankton's concentration
Explains: mercury is stored in tissue and not excreted, and each predator eats many prey, so it builds up at each level (biomagnification)

earns.answer: Mercury rises about 10 times at each step up the chain: 0.002 ppm in plankton, 0.02 in small fish and 0.2 in pike, which is 0.2 / 0.002 = 100 times the plankton's concentration. Mercury is stored in fat and muscle and is not excreted, and each predator eats many prey over its life, so the mercury from all of them builds up. That is biomagnification.
earns.why: It gives the factor at each level, the overall factor and the mechanism.

misses.answer: The pike has the most mercury because it is the biggest fish.
misses.why: Size is not the reason; it gives no numbers and never explains why the concentration multiplies up the chain.

prompts.title: Cutting a town's landfill waste
prompts.context: A town's landfill will be full in five years. A third of the town's waste is food and yard waste. The town wants a solution other than building a new landfill.
prompts.prompt: Propose a solution that fits these constraints and explain how it works.
checklist: Proposes a solution other than a new landfill, aimed at the food and yard waste (for example, curbside composting)
Explains how it works: diverts the waste, which decomposes into compost
Ties it to the five-year limit or the share of the waste

earns.answer: Start curbside collection of food and yard waste and send it to a compost site. Decomposers turn it into compost, so about a third of the town's waste no longer goes to the landfill, which makes the landfill last much longer.
earns.why: It fits the constraint, targets the third of the waste, and explains how it is diverted.

misses.answer: Tell the people in the town to recycle more.
misses.why: It is vague, and recycling does not deal with food and yard waste, the third named.

solution.label: Solution
options: curbside collection of food and yard waste for composting
burn the waste in an open pit

why.1: The town wants something other than a new landfill.
why.2: Open burning is not an accepted way to reduce waste.

how.label: How it works
options: decomposers turn the waste into compost, so it never reaches the landfill
it makes the waste weigh more
it hides the waste from view

why.1: Composting reduces, not increases, the mass sent away.
why.2: Hiding waste is not reducing it.

prompts.title: The variables in a toxicity test
prompts.context: Researchers give groups of 20 water fleas different concentrations of a pesticide (0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 mg/L) and count how many die in 48 hours (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables and describe the purpose of the 0 mg/L group.
checklist: Independent variable: pesticide concentration
Dependent variable: the number (or percent) of water fleas that die
The 0 mg/L group is the control: a baseline to compare against, showing deaths from other causes

earns.answer: The independent variable is the pesticide concentration, from 0 to 8 mg/L. The dependent variable is the number of water fleas that die in 48 hours. The 0 mg/L group is the control: it shows how many die without pesticide, so the deaths caused by the pesticide can be told apart from deaths from other causes.
earns.why: Both variables, and the control with its purpose.

misses.answer: The independent variable is the water fleas, and the 0 group is to compare.
misses.why: Water fleas are the organisms tested, not a variable, and "to compare" does not say compare what.

prompts.title: Protecting the ozone layer
prompts.prompt: Describe a policy that reduced ozone depletion and explain how it worked.
checklist: Names a policy: the Montreal Protocol, an international treaty that phased out CFCs
Explains how it works: fewer CFCs reach the stratosphere, so less chlorine destroys ozone
Does not confuse it with greenhouse policy

earns.answer: The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty that phased out the production of CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals. With fewer CFCs reaching the stratosphere, less chlorine is released by ultraviolet light to break down ozone, so the ozone layer is slowly recovering.
earns.why: A named policy and the chain from fewer CFCs to less ozone destroyed.

misses.answer: Cutting carbon dioxide emissions so the ozone hole closes.
misses.why: Carbon dioxide does not destroy ozone; CFCs do, and the answer names no policy.

type.label: A policy is
options: an international treaty that phased out CFCs

why.1: That is a technology that followed the treaty.
why.2: Carbon dioxide does not destroy ozone.

how.label: It works because
options: less chlorine from CFCs reaches the stratosphere to break down ozone
it traps more heat near the surface
it makes more ultraviolet light reach the ground

why.1: Trapping heat is the greenhouse effect, a different process.
why.2: Protecting ozone lets less ultraviolet reach the ground, not more.

prompts.title: Why warming raises sea level
prompts.prompt: Explain two ways that a warming climate raises sea level.
checklist: Thermal expansion: seawater expands as it warms, taking up more volume
Melting land ice (glaciers and ice sheets) adds new water to the ocean
Does not credit melting sea ice, which floats and barely changes sea level

earns.answer: First, as the ocean absorbs heat, seawater expands and takes up more volume, so sea level rises (thermal expansion). Second, warming melts glaciers and ice sheets on land, such as Greenland's, and that water flows into the ocean, adding to its volume. Melting sea ice does not count, since it already floats in the water it displaces.
earns.why: Two correct causes, each with its mechanism, and it rules out sea ice.

misses.answer: The ice caps and sea ice melt and make the oceans rise.
misses.why: Sea ice melting does not raise sea level, and thermal expansion is missing.

prompts.title: Carbon dioxide and temperature
prompts.context: Atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperature compared with the 1951-1980 average (rounded, similar to NOAA and NASA records): 1960, 317 ppm and 0.0 °C; 1990, 354 ppm and 0.4 °C; 2020, 414 ppm and 1.0 °C.
prompts.prompt: Describe the relationship in the data and explain it.
checklist: Describes it with numbers: as carbon dioxide rose by 97 ppm, temperature rose by 1.0 °C
Notes both rose faster after 1990
Explains: carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emits it, trapping heat

earns.answer: As carbon dioxide rose from 317 to 414 ppm, a rise of 97 ppm, the temperature anomaly rose from 0.0 to 1.0 °C, and both rose faster after 1990. Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation given off by Earth's surface and re-emits some of it back down, so more carbon dioxide traps more heat in the lower atmosphere.
earns.why: The trend with numbers, the speed-up, and the infrared mechanism.

misses.answer: More carbon dioxide destroys the ozone layer, which makes it hotter.
misses.why: That confuses the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion; carbon dioxide traps infrared, it does not destroy ozone.

prompts.title: A hypothesis about acid and shells
prompts.context: A lab grows young clams in seawater at pH 8.1, 7.9 and 7.7 for eight weeks and measures their shell mass (invented study for practice).
prompts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis for this experiment.
checklist: Names the change: lower seawater pH
Names the measure: shell mass
Gives a direction for the result: an increase or a decrease
Gives a reason: lower pH means fewer carbonate ions for building calcium carbonate shells

earns.answer: If the seawater pH is lowered, then the clams' shell mass will decrease, because more acidic water has fewer carbonate ions, which clams need to build calcium carbonate shells.
earns.why: Change, measure, direction and the carbonate reason.

misses.answer: The pH of the water will affect the shells.
misses.why: "Affect" has no direction and no reason.

why.1: Food is not the variable.
why.2: Temperature is held constant here; pH changes.

why.1: Acidic water makes shell building harder, so mass should fall.
why.2: "Change" gives no direction; a hypothesis says which way.

because.label: because ...
options: acidic water has fewer carbonate ions for building shells

why.1: Hunger is not the mechanism.
why.2: A preference is not a mechanism.

prompts.title: Controlling an invasive mussel
prompts.context: Zebra mussels are spreading from lake to lake, carried on boats. The state will not use chemicals in the lakes.
prompts.prompt: Propose a solution that fits this constraint and explain how it works.
checklist: Proposes a solution with no chemicals in the lakes (for example, required boat inspections and washing stations)
Explains how it works: removes mussels and larvae from boats before they enter a new lake
Targets the stated pathway: boats

earns.answer: Require boats to be inspected, drained and washed with hot water at stations at every boat ramp. Hot water kills mussels and larvae on the hulls and in bilge water, so boats cannot carry them to new lakes, which prevents the spread with no chemical in the lakes.
earns.why: It fits the constraint, targets boats, and explains how it stops the spread.

misses.answer: Kill the zebra mussels with a pesticide.
misses.why: The state will not use chemicals in the lakes, so the answer ignores the constraint.

solution.label: Solution
options: require boat inspections and hot-water washing at ramps
add a pesticide to the lakes

why.1: The state will not use chemicals.
why.2: Not practical, and it does not fit a stated constraint.

how.label: How it works
options: hot water kills mussels and larvae on boats before they reach a new lake

why.1: Dislike is not a mechanism.
why.2: Washing boats does not warm lakes.
